lead: A process control loop holds one physical variable — oven temperature, tank level, line pressure — at a set point the operator chooses. The loop measures the variable, compares it with the set point, and uses a power converter as the muscle that pushes the process back. Such loops run heat-treatment furnaces, boiler drums, water tanks and chemical reactors. A plating bath held at 60 °C all shift is one example.
prereq: You need: Unit 5 for phase-angle and integral-cycle AC controllers, and Unit 2 for controlled rectifiers feeding DC drives.

sections.h3: The loop: sensor, transmitter, controller, actuator

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach process control inside a power electronics course. Four parts form the loop, joined one way and closed by feedback.

items: Sensor: PT100 resistance thermometer, thermocouple, float switch or pressure transducer.
Transmitter: converts the reading to 4–20 mA. Current survives long cables, and 4 mA is a live zero, so 0 mA means a broken wire, not a cold oven.
Controller: compares the measurement with the set point and outputs 0–100 %.
Actuator: the power stage — thyristor power controller, solid-state relay, contactor, variable-frequency drive or valve.

blocks.text: On-off control switches fully inside a band and lets the temperature cycle. Proportional control makes the output proportional to the error; the proportional band is the error span that sweeps the output from 0 to 100 %. Integral action removes the steady error. Derivative action damps overshoot.
A heater is the simplest load. P = V_rms²/R, so the controller only sets the RMS voltage across R.
On-off control uses a contactor: cheap, but cycles last minutes, temperature swings widely and contacts wear.

Phase-angle control fires the thyristor at angle α after each zero crossing. Output moves smoothly every half cycle, suiting fast loads such as infrared lamps, at the cost of harmonics and radio interference.

Integral-cycle (burst) control gates whole mains cycles at zero crossings over a fixed period, often 0.4 s, which is 20 cycles at 50 Hz. Current stays nearly sinusoidal, but the heater receives bursts of full power.

blocks.where: V_rms is the RMS output voltage, Vs is the RMS supply voltage, α is the firing angle in radians with 0 ≤ α ≤ π, and the load is resistive.

sections.h3: Sizing the heater control and the rest of the plant

items: From the rating, R = V²/P: 2 kW at 230 V gives R = 26.45 Ω and full-load current P/V = 8.70 A.
Pick thyristors for at least twice that RMS current and for the peak voltage √2 × 230 = 325 V, plus margin.
Add a fast fuse and a heatsink; one thyristor drops about 1 V, so it dissipates roughly 9 W at 8.70 A.
Take the 4–20 mA measurement into the controller and use its 0–100 % output as the firing angle or duty cycle.

blocks.text: A PLC scans inputs, runs ladder logic and drives outputs; SCADA shows the same data to the operator as trends and alarms. Optocouplers or relays isolate the sensor circuit and the 4–20 mA loop from the power circuit, so a shorted heater cannot destroy the controller (gate drive: Unit 1).

A variable-frequency drive holds V/f constant so motor flux stays fixed as speed changes, using the inverter of Unit 4; a DC drive takes armature voltage from a controlled rectifier (Unit 2). Four-quadrant operation lets a drive motor or brake in either direction, so a crane can lower a load under control. Fans, pumps, conveyors and extruders are the usual plant loads.

spec.title: Temperature control loop
spec.aria: A set point and a measured oven temperature meet in a PID controller that drives a thyristor power controller, which sets the heater's firing angle.

examples.question: A 2 kW, 230 V heater is fed from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply through a thyristor AC controller. The load is resistive. Find R, and the firing angle and RMS current at 50 % and at 25 % power.
steps: Power fraction p = (V_rms/Vs)², so V_rms = Vs√p.
examples.answer: R = 26.45 Ω; at 50 % power α = 90° and I_rms = 6.15 A; at 25 % power α = 113.8° and I_rms = 4.35 A.

traps: Controller output is not the firing angle: 50 % output is α = 90° on a phase-angle controller but a 50 % duty cycle on an integral-cycle one.
Heater power follows RMS current, P = I_rms²R, not average current.
4 mA is zero, not 0 mA; a 0 mA reading is a broken loop.
Integral-cycle control cuts harmonics but still thermal-cycles the element if the period is long.

quiz.q: Name the four parts of a process control loop.
Why is 4–20 mA used instead of 0–20 mA?
quiz.a: 4 mA is a live zero, so a 0 mA reading means a broken wire and cannot be confused with a true zero.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of integral-cycle control over phase-angle control.
quiz.a: Switching at zero crossings gives almost no harmonics; the heater receives bursts of full power and the element still cycles thermally.

quiz.q: A 1 kW, 230 V heater runs at 50 % power through a phase-angle controller. Find R and I_rms.
An oven overshoots each time the set point steps up. Which controller action damps this, and what does it act on?
quiz.a: Derivative action; it responds to the rate of change of the error, not to its size.

quiz.q: A crane lowers a load steadily. Which drive quadrants are in use, and why?
quiz.a: The load overhauls the motor, so torque opposes rotation: braking operation in quadrant II or IV, with energy returned to the DC bus or dumped in a chopper resistor.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern plants the loop often moves into the drive: a pump's variable-frequency drive closes the pressure loop internally and the PLC sends only a set point over a fieldbus. Self-tuning PID and model predictive control sit above this layer. Search 'burst firing thyristor controller', '4–20 mA current loop' and 'four-quadrant drive'.
